meta.title: Who really said "Knowledge itself is power"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Francis Bacon wrote it. “Knowledge itself is power” renders his Latin “ipsa scientia potestas est” from Meditationes Sacrae (1597).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Knowledge itself is power'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Bacon: “knowledge itself is power” translates “ipsa scientia potestas est” from Meditationes Sacrae (1597), essay “Of Heresies.”

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1561–1626 · English philosopher, statesman & pioneer of the scientific method
answer.sourceLine: This is genuinely Bacon. In his Meditationes Sacrae (1597), in the essay “De Hæresibus” (Of Heresies), he wrote “Nam et ipsa scientia potestas est” — rendered in the standard Spedding edition as “For also knowledge itself is power.” The familiar “knowledge itself is power” is a faithful translation, the ‘itself’ carrying the Latin ipsa. The clipped three-word form “Knowledge is power” is an editors’ paraphrase, and the near-identical maxim “scientia potentia est” is Hobbes’s.

source.excerpt: Nam et ipsa scientia potestas est. — For also knowledge itself is power.
trail: The line comes from Bacon’s Meditationes Sacrae (1597); Wikiquote’s sourced entry gives the Latin “Nam et ipsa scientia potestas est” and the English “For knowledge itself is power” — see Wikiquote.
The standard scholarly translation, “For also knowledge itself is power,” appears in the Spedding, Ellis & Heath edition of the collected Works (vol. 7, p. 253).
Bacon’s Latin ipsa scientia potestas est should not be confused with Thomas Hobbes’s later scientia potentia est (1668 Leviathan), as Wikipedia details.
source.excerptNote: The Latin ipsa (‘itself’) is what distinguishes Bacon’s phrasing; it survives in the English “knowledge itself is power.”
source.rightsNote: The source work, Meditationes Sacrae, was first published in 1597, and the standard English translation was published in the Spedding–Ellis–Heath edition (1887–1901) — both long before the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff. The wording is freely reproducible.

author.bio: Sir Francis Bacon, 1st Viscount St Alban, was an English philosopher, essayist and statesman who rose to Lord Chancellor under James I. He is remembered as a founder of the empirical, experimental approach to knowledge — the “Baconian method” — set out in works such as the Novum Organum (1620). The devotional Meditationes Sacrae (1597), where this line appears, was published alongside the first edition of his celebrated Essays.

misattribution.heading: The wording, sorted out
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Bacon is correct — but two related confusions travel with this quote.

items.why: The clipped three-word slogan is an editors’ summary, not Bacon’s literal words; his phrase is the fuller ipsa scientia potestas est, “knowledge itself is power,” per todayinsci.
The near-identical Latin maxim was written by Hobbes in the 1668 Latin Leviathan (“Scientia potentia est, sed parva”) — a different phrase from Bacon’s, as Wikipedia notes.

misattribution.truthLine: The exact line asked about — “knowledge itself is power” — is authentically Bacon’s, from Meditationes Sacrae (1597), rendering his Latin “Nam et ipsa scientia potestas est.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Bacon uses the phrase not as a boast about worldly command but inside a religious argument: heretics err, he says, by imagining a gap between the extent of God’s power and the extent of God’s knowledge — “for knowledge itself is power” in God, the two being one. Over the following century the line was lifted out of that theological setting and became a banner for the empirical, science-as-mastery worldview Bacon himself did so much to launch.
